# Zechariah 1: Research Notes

**Gaps:** I didn't get to any pages from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org, and none of my searches turned up prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. The few Catholic and Church Father points below come secondhand through Protestant commentaries. The Enduring Word page I read was cut off partway through vv. 18–21, so I took its comments on those verses from search snippets.

## Part 1: Verse by verse (the traditional reading)

**v. 1**
- Guzik says Zechariah worked after the return from exile. His career is dated by a Persian ruler, Darius, because Israel and Judah had no king in this period. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/
- Guzik dates the prophecy to October–November 520 B.C. That is two months after Haggai's first message. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/
- Guzik notes that the name Zechariah means "the LORD remembers," which suits a prophet of restoration. He also links this Zechariah to Jesus' words in Matthew 23:35. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/
- Clarke identifies the king as Darius Hystaspes. He says Zechariah began prophesying two months after Haggai, and that the two spellings of "Iddo" are the same name. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Ellicott places this message a few weeks after Haggai's promise that the latter glory of the temple would be greater than the former. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html

**v. 2**
- Clarke says God was angry with the fathers for their ingratitude, idolatry, wickedness and general rebellion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Ellicott notes that the prophet counts himself among those whose "fathers" sinned. He says this verse is the basis for the call to repent that follows. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- The Pulpit Commentary points to the fallen kingdom, the exile and the ruined land around them as proof of God's anger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/1.htm
- Guzik stresses that the people being warned were the committed remnant who had come back. Even they needed this warning some 18 years after returning. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/

**v. 3**
- Guzik lists why the people felt God was far away: a desolate land, hard work, poverty, drought and enemies. His reply is that if we feel far from God, God is not the one who moved. He links the verse to James 4:8. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/
- Ellicott says the words don't have to mean the people had recently fallen away. They mean the more sincerely the people turned, the more fully God's mercy would be shown. He quotes Wordsworth comparing Zechariah to John the Baptist. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says "LORD of Hosts," repeated three times, stands for God's almighty power and unlimited resources. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-3.htm
- Gill suggests the threefold "LORD of hosts" may point to the three Persons of the Trinity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-3.htm
- The traditions read the "if you return, I will return" pattern quite differently. See Part 2.

**v. 4**
- Ellicott says the "former prophets" are those who preached before the exile, while Jerusalem was still inhabited and doing well. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- Benson, as quoted on Bible Hub, reads "be not as your fathers" as "do not persist in impenitence as your fathers did." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-3.htm

**v. 5**
- Clarke says the fathers died in the wars with Assyria and Babylon. The prophets who spoke to them are dead too, but their predictions remain, and the way events matched them proves God sent them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Ellicott reads the verse as a back-and-forth. The prophet asks where the fathers are; the people answer that the prophets died as well. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- A comment on Bible Hub puts it this way: the preachers and hearers died, but God's word did not. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-3.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott says the point is that the prophets' words really did come true for the fathers, as the fathers themselves admitted. He traces this reading to the rabbi Rav in the Talmud. He rejects the alternative reading, "the light of prophecy is dying out," because it breaks the prophet's argument. He takes "returned" to mean "repented," and links the fathers' confession to Lamentations 2:17. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- Guzik says God's word outlasted both the prophets and the fathers. He adds that Zechariah wanted the people to rebuild their relationship with God, not only the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/

**v. 7**
- Clarke says Shebat falls in part of our February, about three months after the first message and two months after temple building restarted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Ellicott says the month names come from Assyria and Babylon. He takes all the visions of 1:7–6:15 as seen in a single night. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html

**v. 8**
- Clarke takes the "man" to be the Lord Jesus appearing before his incarnation, and the night to stand for the Jews' suffering. In his view the red horse means war, the myrtles mean peace, and the horse colours may show ranks of angels. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Guzik says the man is the Angel of the LORD and "no doubt" Jesus before Bethlehem. He reasons from John 1:18: no one has seen the Father, so a visible appearance of God must be the Son. He sees the myrtle as possibly a symbol of Israel and quotes Boice on its fragrance when crushed. He thinks the horses don't match the four horsemen of Revelation 6. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/
- Ellicott says this was a waking vision, not a dream. He holds that the grammar makes the man and the Angel of the LORD (v. 11) the same person. He surveys several theories about the colours and myrtles, calls them all guesswork, and suggests a myrtle grove in a hollow is simply where scouts would naturally stop. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- Keil & Delitzsch read the myrtles as God's people or land, and the "hollow" as the low state they had fallen into. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-11.htm

**v. 9**
- Ellicott says Zechariah is speaking to the interpreting angel, whose job runs through all the visions. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- Clarke says this angel is distinct from the riders. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Bob Utley on bible.org notes that "my lord" here is *adoni*, an ordinary title ("master"), not God's covenant name. https://bible.org/seriespage/zechariah-1

**v. 10**
- Wesley and Poole take the horsemen to be angels serving God's providence in running the world. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/1-10.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-10.htm
- Clarke says they act as guardians of the land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Guzik quotes Baldwin: like Persian kings with swift mounted messengers, the Lord knows all about the nations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/

**v. 11**
- Clarke says the Persian empire was at peace while the Jews were still suffering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Ellicott calls this peace a self-confident security. Haggai had foretold that God would overthrow kingdoms, and that had not begun yet. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- Guzik says it was "not the right kind of peace," because the nations were comfortable while God's people suffered. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/

**v. 12**
- Clarke identifies this speaker as the Lord Jesus, always the only mediator and intercessor. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Matthew Henry contrasts the two: the angels only report, but the Angel among the myrtles prays. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/1-12.html
- **Seventy years.** Clarke counts from the temple's destruction to this vision. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html Ellicott says "seventy" is often a round number. He thinks it can't be Jeremiah's 70 years, since about 88 years had passed by then, and probably refers to about 68 years since 588 B.C. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html Keil notes the 70 years were "completed twice." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-12.htm

**v. 13**
- Ellicott says the LORD answers the interpreting angel rather than the one who prayed, so the comfort passes to the prophet. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- Keil cites Hengstenberg: the Angel of the LORD asked so that comfort would reach the prophet and, through him, the nation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-10.htm

**v. 14**
- Guzik says the Hebrew word for "zealous/jealous" comes from the idea of a face flushing red with deep feeling. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/
- Ellicott says the verb tense shows God had already shown this jealous love by bringing the people home. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- Clarke reads it as strong love for his people and anger at their enemies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html

**v. 15**
- The Pulpit Commentary says God was angry only in measure, punishing like a parent. Some take "a little" to mean "for a little while." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/1.htm
- Ellicott says the nations didn't just punish Israel; they wanted to wipe it out (compare Isaiah 47:6). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- Clarke says the nations went far beyond God's purpose through oppression and cruelty, and would now suffer in turn. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Poole, in a vivid picture: "I would prune, but they struck at the root." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-15.htm
- Guzik follows the NKJV wording: the nations helped "with evil intent." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/

**v. 16**
- Clarke says God had come in judgment before but now comes in mercy. The greatest mercy is the rebuilt house of the Lord, and the measuring line marks out the city's bounds. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Ellicott links the line to Zechariah 2:1–2. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html

**v. 17**
- Ellicott says "spread abroad" here means "filled to overflowing." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- Clarke takes it to mean the ruined cities of Judea would be lived in again. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Guzik notes the temple was finished about four years after this prophecy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/

**vv. 18–19 (the four horns)**
- Horns stand for power. The Pulpit Commentary reads "four" as hostile powers from every side. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-18.htm
- Clarke gives two options. Either four specific powers (Assyrians, Persians, Chaldeans, Egyptians) or enemies from the four points of the compass. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Ellicott argues that "have scattered" is past tense. So the horns can't include Greece, which did not yet exist. If they are four kingdoms, they must be Assyria, Egypt, Babylon and Medo-Persia. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- Keil, citing Jerome, Hengstenberg and others, links the horns to Daniel's four empires. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-18.htm
- Guzik suggests Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome, if "scattering" is meant in a broad prophetic sense. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/
- Coffman links the horns to the beast of Revelation 13. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/1-18.html
- Gill reports Cocceius's view: four kings, applicable to "antichristian states, Pagan and Papal." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-18.htm

**vv. 20–21 (the four craftsmen)**
- Ellicott says the Hebrew word means "workmen" in general. He prefers not to name them; they simply picture the overthrow of these nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html
- Clarke reports Calmet's list: Nabopolassar, Cyrus, Alexander and Ptolemy. He also prints a reader's suggestion that the word means angelic "watchers." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- Matthew Henry says that for every horn God has a hand to saw it off. He mentions that some see Zerubbabel, Joshua, Ezra and Nehemiah here. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/1-18.html
- Gill thinks those four leaders were too minor a match. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-21.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: for every enemy, God provides a power able to destroy it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Zec/Zec_001.cfm

## Part 2: Where the traditions differ

**v. 3: Does "return to me" show that people can turn by their own power?**
- **Wesleyan/Methodist (Clarke):** The command shows the people *had power* to return. God gives that power and will require it. No one is lost for lack of power to turn. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html
- **Reformed (Calvin):** He calls the use of this verse to prove free will "puerile sophistry." God's "returning" here means outward blessing, not the Spirit helping free will. God's commands show what we owe, not what we can do. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/1-3.html
- **Calvinist Baptist (Gill):** Turning is "not the condition of what follows." God's promise is the motive and encouragement to turn. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/1-3.html
- **A middle position (Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary):** They quote the saying that "Turn to me" reminds us of our freedom, while "Turn us, Lord" admits our need of grace that comes first. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-3.htm

**vv. 8–12: Who is the Angel of the LORD?**
- **Seen as the pre-incarnate Christ:** Clarke (Wesleyan) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-1.html ; Guzik https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-1/ ; J. Vernon McGee https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/1-10.html ; Poole https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-12.htm
- **Calvin** thinks it "probable" that this is Christ the Mediator, but allows it could be any angel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-12.htm
- **Keil** holds that the angel praying to God no more disproves his oneness with God than Jesus' prayer in John 17 disproves Jesus' divinity. Unlike Ellicott, though, Keil thinks the rider on the red horse is a different figure from the angel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-12.htm
- **Benson** sees an angel of higher rank, not explicitly God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/1-10.html
- **Utley (bible.org):** He notes that many hold the Christ view, but says v. 12 shows the angel is distinct from the Lord of hosts. https://bible.org/seriespage/zechariah-1

## Part 3: Other views

- **Catholic (secondhand):** Barnes cites the Council of Trent on v. 3. "Turn to me" is said to remind us of our freedom; "turn us" admits that God's grace goes before us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-3.htm Calvin attacks what he calls the "Papist" free-will reading of the same verse. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/1-3.html
- **Catholic translations (v. 12):** The Douay-Rheims renders the end of the verse "this is now the seventieth year." https://biblehub.com/zechariah/1-12.htm
- **Latin Vulgate (v. 15):** It translates "at ease" as "wealthy," as if the nations' riches made them self-confident. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/1.htm
- **Church Fathers (secondhand):** Jerome is cited for the four-empires view of the horns. Cyril says a horn in Scripture means strength and usually pride. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/1-18.htm
- **Modern critical caution:** Ellicott calls it "most uncritical" to read the horse colours through Revelation. He treats many symbolic details as setting rather than coded meaning. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-1.html Utley lays out the two main ways of dating the 70 years (605–539 B.C. or 586–516 B.C.), and raises whether "seventy" might be a symbolic number. https://bible.org/seriespage/zechariah-1
